questionText:
Read the following excerpt on overuse injuries and specialization hazards in youth sports and answer the questions that follow:

Overuse injuries account for nearly 50% of all sports injuries among adolescent athletes, driven by excessive training volume, insufficient recovery, and premature single-sport specialization. Because adolescent bones, tendons, and cartilage are growing rapidly, they are uniquely vulnerable at traction apophyses. A common traction apophysitis is 'Osgood-Schlatter Disease'—repetitive micro-trauma from the patellar tendon pulling on the unossified tibial tuberosity during running and jumping in basketball or soccer, causing pain, swelling, and a prominent bony bump below the knee. In the foot, 'Sever's Disease' (calcaneal apophysitis) involves repetitive Achilles tendon traction on the posterior heel growth plate in young runners. In youth baseball pitchers, 'Little League Elbow' (medial epicondylar apophysitis) results from repetitive valgus stress during overhead throwing.
